memory_update.text: Politics theme should be decomposed into policy demand channels: defense acquisition, critical minerals, domestic manufacturing, infrastructure/grid, and regulated supply-chain compliance.

Most important hidden chokepoint appears to be lower-tier defense industrial base suppliers, because public evidence indicates DoD and primes lose visibility below early tiers and these suppliers face financing constraints.

Missile and solid-rocket-motor production chain is a high-priority node because some critical systems have limited active production lines and require qualified energetics, nozzles, ablatives, and specialty materials.
Rare-earth and magnet exposure should be framed around compliant feedstock qualification and usable defense supply, not only mine output or nominal magnet capacity.

Watch for multiyear procurement, Defense Production Act awards, domestic-content rules, rare-earth waiver decisions, and contract language requiring supply-chain mapping or pass-through funding to lower tiers.

Need primary-source verification from NDAA text, DoD contract awards, DPA Title III announcements, company filings, backlog disclosures, and customer qualification evidence before mapping public tickers to bottleneck nodes.

Need to distinguish broad political beneficiaries from true chokepoints by checking whether suppliers have scarce qualifications, funded capacity expansion, sole-source or few-source positions, and pricing power.
Underfollowed political-theme value may hide in suppliers, distributors, certification/compliance providers, regulated assets, and niche tools rather than in obvious mega-cap policy winners.

NEU should be carried forward as the highest-priority underfollowed relationship in this chunk because AMPAC ammonium perchlorate exposure maps directly to solid-rocket-motor input constraints while being hidden inside a petroleum-additives issuer.
KRMN and PKE should be grouped under solid-rocket-motor components/materials, but both require program-level and qualification evidence before they can be treated as true chokepoint suppliers.

MP, NEO.TO, and LYC.AX should be mapped to the rare-earth compliance chain where the key diligence variable is qualified non-Chinese feedstock, separation, and magnet/material qualification rather than headline resource tonnage.

UAMY remains a speculative_shadow strategic-minerals candidate: the political-policy fit is strong, but the investable relationship depends on primary confirmation of DLA obligations, recurring demand, capacity, margins, liquidity, and dilution risk.

MRCY and DCO should remain in the underfollowed sub-tier defense supplier lane but should be downgraded unless filings prove backlog quality, program specificity, constrained supplier status, and margin recovery or pricing power.

Layer 2B still lacks primary SEC filing validation for NEU/AMPAC, UAMY, KRMN, PKE, MRCY, and DCO; next layer should prioritize 10-K/10-Q, earnings-call, DPA Title III, DLA, FPDS, SAM.gov, and contract-obligation evidence.

Need to distinguish announced award ceilings, appropriated dollars, obligated contract funds, delivery orders, backlog, and revenue recognition before assigning revenue sensitivity to any defense-policy candidate.

Need current market capitalization, liquidity, analyst coverage, valuation, short interest, and borrow availability checks before any Layer 3 prioritization; this output is research mapping only and not a buy/sell recommendation.

MYRG maps to grid/transmission/public-spending execution capacity; relationship remains a hypothesis until backlog, utility capex linkage, labor constraints, and public-funded project conversion are verified from filings.
PRIM maps to specialty contracting for grid, utility, renewable, energy, and industrial infrastructure; must verify backlog mix, federally supported projects, and margin quality before upgrading.

DSGX maps to customs, tariff, denied-party screening, and supply-chain compliance software; potential regulation-created recurring revenue beneficiary if filings confirm trade-compliance sensitivity and pricing power.
EXPO maps to testing, engineering, safety, forensic, environmental, and regulatory complexity; exposure is plausible but diffuse and requires case-mix validation.

CACI maps to federal mission IT, cyber, intelligence, electronic warfare, and defense modernization; verify bookings, funded backlog, classified mix, recompetes, and continuing-resolution sensitivity.
SAIC maps to federal IT and defense services but may have weaker Serenity bottleneck quality if growth is labor-driven, recompete-prone, or margin-constrained.

PSN maps to hybrid critical infrastructure, cyber, space, missile-defense, and federal engineering services; categorization complexity may hide exposure but requires funded-backlog and margin validation.
BAH should remain a reference leader for federal AI, analytics, cyber, and mission consulting demand, not the primary underfollowed alpha candidate.
LHX should be used as a reference anchor for Aerojet, solid rocket motor, missile propulsion, and sub-tier energetics/component pull-through.
NOC should be used as a reference anchor for missile products and solid rocket motor bottleneck mapping, especially where sub-tier energetics or qualified inputs may constrain deliveries.

Company-level primary evidence is missing for all underfollowed tickers in this chunk. Next layer should pull latest 10-K/10-Q, investor presentations, earnings transcripts, awarded-contract data, backlog disclosures, and segment margins.

Need to distinguish announced policy dollars, appropriated budget authority, obligated funds, award ceilings, funded backlog, and actual revenue recognition for infrastructure and federal-services tickers.

Need market-pricing checks for MYRG, PRIM, DSGX, EXPO, CACI, SAIC, PSN, BAH, LHX, and NOC: market cap, valuation, revenue growth expectations, analyst coverage, liquidity, and whether the politics theme is already embedded in consensus.

TMC maps to the Politics theme only through a speculative-shadow critical-minerals supply-response pathway, not through a currently verified defense procurement, processing, magnet, or lower-tier industrial-base bottleneck.

Primary-source validation is required for TMC: SEC filings, regulatory/permitting status, environmental litigation, commercial production timeline, binding offtakes, financing, government support, and any explicit eligibility under U.S. or allied critical-minerals programs.

Need to test whether seabed-derived minerals would satisfy domestic, allied, defense, battery, ESG, traceability, and customer qualification requirements; without this, TMC remains policy optionality rather than a Serenity chokepoint.

Need market-pricing checks for TMC before later layers: current market cap, liquidity, dilution risk, financing runway, short interest, valuation versus pre-revenue status, and sensitivity to permitting headlines.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Layer 2A industry-chain map for the broad Politics theme. The strongest investable chain is not generic election exposure but policy-driven reconfiguration of defense, critical minerals, domestic manufacturing, infrastructure, and regulated supply chains. The key Serenity/chokepoint insight is that political demand often enters through large appropriations and prime contractors, but bottleneck value may hide lower in the chain: sub-tier defense suppliers, qualified energetics inputs, rare-earth/magnet feedstock qualification, skilled labor, domestic processing, government-owned industrial capacity, certification gates, and small suppliers with weak balance sheets. No buy/sell view is implied.

supply_chain_map.node: Defense appropriations and acquisition demand signal
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Political decisions on budgets, multiyear procurement, and acquisition authorities determine whether defense suppliers receive enough demand visibility to invest in new capacity. The JPMorgan defense industrial base report states that government acquisition decisions shape the demand signals that determine whether industry invests and expands.

Prime contractors translate political spending into production programs, but they are not necessarily the scarce layer. The bottleneck may sit in the sub-tier network beneath them where visibility, financing, and capacity are weaker.

CNAS describes lower-tier suppliers as thinly capitalized, dependent on few contracts, and exposed to delays in appropriations or contracts. DoD supply chains can span five to six tiers, while visibility is often lost beyond tier two. This makes lower-tier suppliers a high-priority hidden bottleneck zone.

supply_chain_map.node: Solid rocket motor and missile-production chain
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Missile, munitions, hypersonic, and air-defense production are politically sensitive areas where procurement growth can run into physical production limits. The JPMorgan report notes single active production lines for some critical systems, including large-diameter solid rocket motors.

Energetic materials, oxidizers, propellants, and related specialty chemicals can be hard to qualify, dangerous to handle, environmentally regulated, and difficult to expand quickly. These inputs may be more capacity-constrained than final assembly.

supply_chain_map.node: Rocket-motor nozzles, ablatives, composite materials, and thermal-protection components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Missile-production growth depends on qualified material and component suppliers. These are niche, qualification-heavy categories where low-attention public or private suppliers may hold bottleneck positions.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty metals, aerospace alloys, and qualified materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Defense and aerospace systems require qualified titanium, nickel alloys, high-performance steels, and engineered materials. Long qualification cycles and capacity utilization can create lagged supply constraints even after political demand appears.

Political pressure to reduce dependence on adversarial or concentrated foreign supply chains turns mining, refining, and processing capacity into a policy chokepoint. The JPMorgan report highlights growing focus on domestic mineral mining and refining.

The critical issue may not be mine output alone but whether feedstock is legally compliant, non-Chinese, and qualified for defense supply chains. External evidence from The Fuse and ForcedAlpha suggests policy is shifting from simple sourcing restrictions toward enforceable supply-chain requirements.

supply_chain_map.node: Permanent magnets and NdFeB magnet supply chain
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Defense systems require rare-earth magnets, but policy deadlines and qualification requirements can create mismatches between nominal capacity and usable defense-compliant supply. This is a likely hidden bottleneck because the market may count mines while missing qualified magnet/feedstock capacity.

Defense, aerospace, and critical-mineral supply chains cannot switch suppliers quickly. Qualification, cybersecurity, domestic-content compliance, controlled-material rules, and program-specific approvals can make the certified supplier base more scarce than the physical production base.

supply_chain_map.node: Organic Industrial Base and government-owned facilities
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The JPMorgan report notes underinvestment in the Organic Industrial Base and reduced surge capacity. Political funding can repair this, but execution depends on facilities, tooling, workforce, and procurement reform.

Sub-tier defense production requires specialized machinists, welders, engineers, energetics workers, quality inspectors, and cleared personnel. Labor shortages can prevent procurement dollars from converting into output.
Policy-driven demand requires plant capacity, test equipment, tooling, safe handling systems, environmental controls, and inspection tools. These are slower to expand than budget authority.

Political focus on supply-chain security and domestic manufacturing can benefit secure electronics, RF systems, mission-processing modules, and trusted suppliers below the prime-contractor layer. This is a potential underfollowed node but requires company-level evidence.

Political spending and industrial-policy programs can raise demand for substations, switchgear, transformers, protection systems, and power-distribution equipment. Bottlenecks may hide in long-lead electrical equipment rather than obvious construction contractors.

Some policy effects reach the market through distributors, integrators, government resellers, and service providers that manage compliance, procurement access, and inventory. These can be overlooked because they are not direct manufacturers.

CNAS emphasizes that vulnerable lower-tier companies often lack capital to front costs while waiting for appropriations or contracts. Financing itself can become a bottleneck unless Congress, primes, or government programs pass funds down the chain.

CNAS notes that DoD and prime contractors often lack visibility beyond early tiers. Tools and processes that map lower-tier dependencies may become politically important, though public-market mapping remains speculative at this stage.
